## Where this sits on the stack

This chapter fixes no new version of anything on the
determinant stack, and neither of its halves, sharing
with a team and archiving with the world, adds a rung.
It still does two things to the stack, and they differ
in kind.

@fig-stack-archiving marks both. Archiving pins the
*input data* layer more tightly than any earlier
chapter, which is the second sense of 'captures' in the
[Conventions](conventions.qmd). The compendium of
@sec-compendium made the data locatable in a team's
repository, which a forge outage or a departed
contributor can erase. A deposit moves them to a
persistent identifier that continues to resolve after
the project ends. The layer is marked as captured here
for that reason, although no new version or byte is
fixed. Stewardship, by contrast, pins nothing new about
the packages or the operating system; the lockfile of
@sec-dependencies and the digest-pinned image of
@sec-containers already did that capturing. What
stewardship does is confirm, using `rang` or an archived
image, that those pins still resolve after they have
aged. It validates layers already captured elsewhere.

## Orientation

The last question a reproducible analysis must answer is
a social and temporal one. Every earlier chapter was
concerned with a single machine and a single analyst. We
saw how to pin the packages (@sec-dependencies), fix the
environment (@sec-containers), and render the report
(@sec-literate). We then saw how to validate the whole
with tests and continuous integration (@sec-verification).
The present chapter concerns what happens when the
analysis must leave that machine. It must first reach
a collaborator down the hall, and eventually reach a
stranger, a reviewer, or the analyst's own future self,
years after the original laptop has been recycled.

Consider a concrete case. A five-person laboratory
runs a multi-site observational cohort. The
principal investigator fixes the computational
environment at the project's start. Over the following
year, one contributor adds survival-analysis packages,
a second adds table-formatting packages for the
manuscript, and a third adds spatial packages for a
geographic sub-study. Each installs freely, on their
own machine, without asking the others' permission.
Two years after the paper appears, a journal requests
the analysis for a reproducibility audit. The original
environment must then be reconstructed from whatever
survives in the repository. Nothing in the
single-analyst workflow of the earlier chapters tells
us how the laboratory should have coordinated during
that year. Nor does it tell us how the compendium should
have been deposited so that the audit could succeed.

These are two distinct problems, and we shall keep
them apart. The first is collaboration: sharing a
compendium with a team while it is under active
development, so that contributors do not drift into
mutually incompatible environments. The second is
archiving and stewardship: depositing the finished
compendium so that it remains findable and executable
long after the project ends, and recovering it when the
pins have decayed. Both sit at the top of the
reproducibility ladder and add no new rung.
Sharing a compendium changes nothing about its
level: an L2 compendium shared with a team is still an
L2 compendium, and a verified L3 compendium deposited
in an archive is still L3. What sharing and archiving
add is the assurance that the level already reached
survives contact with other people and with the
passage of time. That assurance is the subject of this
chapter. Being the last chapter, it is also where we
draw the threads of the whole book together.

We begin with the three judgments that remain the
analyst's own. We then take up sharing with a team
through the two-layer model, and sharing with the world
through archiving, including what changes when the data
are restricted. Stewardship over time, and the recovery
of a decayed environment, follow. Lastly, we consider the
archetypes, a worked example, and a check of this book's
own compendium against a deposit checklist.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: two problems, not one

The laboratory's L2 compendium is shared with a new
contributor, who extends the package layer, and is later
deposited in Zenodo. Does either event change the level
the compendium has reached? What does each event add if
not a level?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

Neither event changes the level. Sharing the compendium
with a new contributor, and depositing it with a DOI, are
both social and temporal acts, not capture acts. The
compendium was L2 before either happened and remains L2
afterward. What sharing adds is that the fixed environment
survives contact with a second person without drifting.
What archiving adds is that the fixed environment survives
the passage of time and the disappearance of the original
machine.
:::
:::

## The analyst's contribution

Before turning to the mechanics, we note that three
judgments in this chapter are the analyst's own, and no
tool makes them.

1. **Where to draw the governance boundary, between
   what the team fixes and what each member may vary.**
   The framework offers the two-layer model as a
   default. However, only a person who understands the
   project can decide which layer a given decision
   belongs to. Fixing too much makes the team rigid and
   slows every contributor; fixing too little lets the
   environment fracture. The base image, the R version,
   the system libraries, and the packages every project
   in the lab uses are almost always the lead's to fix;
   the packages one project's analysis needs are almost
   always the members' to add. The awkward cases in
   between (a version of a system library that one
   sub-study needs and the others do not) are decided
   by the analyst, not the tool.

2. **When to deposit, at what depth, and at what level
   to claim.** An archival deposit is a public and
   permanent act, and the honest disclosure of the
   level reached is part of the deposit. Depositing a
   compendium and labeling it 'reproducible' without
   stating whether it has been verified, or whether the
   environment was pinned by digest or merely by tag,
   misrepresents the work.
   The analyst decides when the compendium is ready and
   which artifacts accompany it. The analyst also decides
   which data the consent and the data-use agreement
   allow to accompany it, and, above all, what the
   accompanying claim honestly says.

3. **Where the work lives, and how dependent that
   choice makes it.** A registry and a forge are
   conveniences, but each is also a dependency on a
   commercial vendor whose terms may change. The
   analyst weighs the convenience of a popular platform
   against the vendor independence of an institutional
   or self-hosted alternative. The analyst does so
   knowing that a compendium tied to a service that
   disappears is a compendium at risk.

::: {.callout-note}
## The vocabulary of this chapter

- **Registry.** A server that stores and distributes
  container images, from which collaborators pull a
  pre-built environment. GitHub Container Registry
  (GHCR) and Docker Hub are the two in common use.
- **Forge.** A platform that hosts a version-controlled
  repository and runs its continuous integration.
  GitHub and GitLab are the two principal forges;
  GitLab is frequently self-hosted by universities.
- **Two-layer team model.** A division of a project
  into a slow-moving environment layer, fixed once by a
  team lead, and a fast-moving package layer, extended
  by every contributor. The environment layer is the
  team image: the operating system, the R version, the
  system libraries, and the packages every project in
  the lab uses, pinned by digest. The package layer is
  the project lockfile.
- **Union model.** The rule that the project lockfile
  records the union of every package any contributor
  has installed, so that a rebuilt image carries what
  the whole team needs, not only what one member used.
- **Persistent identifier (DOI).** A durable, resolvable
  name for a deposited artifact, such as a Digital
  Object Identifier, that continues to resolve even if
  the artifact moves.
- **FAIR.** A set of principles holding that a research
  object should be Findable, Accessible, Interoperable,
  and Reusable, formulated for data and later adapted
  for research software.
- **OCI tarball or SIF file.** A container image exported
  as a single file, checksummable and depositable as an
  archival artifact. An OCI image is exported as a tar
  archive, whereas SIF is the self-contained single-file
  format used by the Apptainer runtime.
- **Zenodo.** A general-purpose research repository,
  operated at CERN, that mints a DOI for any deposited
  file set.
- **Controlled access.** A repository arrangement in
  which data are released only to approved users under
  an agreement, rather than to anyone who downloads.
- **Data-availability statement.** The statement in an
  article or README of what was deposited, where, and
  how any data not deposited may be obtained.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: whose judgment, again

A compendium is ready to deposit, by every mechanical
check: the tests pass, the lockfile is current, the image
builds. Name one judgment from this section that a
checklist still cannot make, and say why it cannot.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

A checklist cannot decide what level to claim in the
accompanying statement. It can confirm that a lockfile and
a Dockerfile exist, which is mechanical. However, it
cannot decide whether the analyst has actually re-run the
pipeline from a clean rebuild and compared the outputs.
Nor can it know what the consent and data-use agreement
permit to accompany the deposit. Those are judgments about this
specific project's history and its governing documents,
and no tool has access to either.
:::
:::

## Sharing with a team: the two-layer model

We begin with collaboration. The design starts from one
observation: the two things a team shares change at
very different rates.
The computational environment (the operating system,
the R version, the system libraries, and the packages
every project in the lab uses) is chosen at most a
handful of times over the life of a project. The set of
packages one project needs, by contrast, changes almost
weekly as the analysis grows. A model that forces both
to be renegotiated on the same schedule will either
freeze the packages to the cadence of the environment,
which is too slow, or churn the environment to the
cadence of the packages, which is too disruptive. The
resolution, adopted by the framework this book uses and
set out by its authors, is to separate the two into
layers with different change rates and different
governance.

**Layer 1 is the environment, and it is lead-governed.**
A designated team lead selects a base image at the
project's start and builds on it a team image carrying
the packages every project in the lab uses, as
@sec-containers sketched. The lead resolves that image
to an immutable content digest and fixes it for every
collaborator. This is the slow-moving half. It
corresponds to pillar one, the
computational environment, and it is where the L1-to-L2
transition of the ladder is secured. The lead builds
this environment once, and the whole team reuses it.
The vignette that describes the pattern calls this
'build once, use everywhere'. It reports that reusing a
pre-built team image reduces the setup of a new project
from the fifteen or twenty minutes of a full build to a
matter of seconds. For reproducibility, the larger gain
is that every collaborator works from the same fixed
floor.

**Layer 2 is the project's package set, and it is
contributor-governed under the union model.** Each
member installs, on top of the team image, the packages
their part of the work requires, freely and without
coordination. The project
lockfile at any moment records the *union* of everything
anyone has installed. The shared image is rebuilt from
that lockfile periodically rather than on every change.
When it is, it carries the full set every contributor
needs, not merely the subset one member happened to use.
A collaborator who pulls the latest main branch and
rebuilds therefore inherits the survival packages, the
table packages, and the spatial packages all at once.
This holds whether or not their own work touches any of
them. This is the fast-moving half, corresponding to
pillar two, and it is governed by every member.

The union model buys the elimination of a common and
maddening failure, the analysis that runs for its author
and nowhere else. The price is a little environmental
bloat. A package installed once for an exploratory
notebook remains in the lockfile for everyone until it
is deliberately removed. In our view this is a sound
trade. On the one hand, the bloat is bounded and
visible, a few extra megabytes in an image that is
already a gigabyte or more, and it can be pruned when it
matters. On the other, the failure it prevents is a
contributor blocked because a colleague forgot to record
a dependency. That is the precise 'works on my machine'
pathology that the whole enterprise exists to abolish.
We would rather carry an unused package than lose a day
to a missing one.

### The Dockerfile, not the image, is the guarantee

The pushed team image is a convenience, a
cache that saves build time; it is *not* the
reproducibility guarantee. The guarantee is the
Dockerfile, together with the lockfile it restores from,
both committed to version control. The reason is that a
pushed image is opaque and impermanent. It is a binary
blob on a registry that may be deleted, or pruned under
a retention policy. It may be pushed for one processor
architecture and silently emulated on another, and it
cannot be inspected line by line to see how it was made.
The Dockerfile is transparent and durable: it is a
text recipe, readable and diffable, that reconstructs
the image from named and pinned inputs. If the registry
vanishes tomorrow, a compendium whose guarantee is the
Dockerfile can be rebuilt; a compendium whose guarantee
was the pushed image cannot.

The framework's vignette makes the same point in a note
that merits restating in our terms. Pushing the image to
a registry is optional, and if the image is not
available, building from the Dockerfile reproduces the
environment. We should qualify that claim, in keeping
with this chapter's own discipline. A rebuild reproduces
the same content (the same base image, R version, and
package versions) only when the base image is pinned by
content digest and the package snapshot is dated, as
@sec-containers urged. A recipe pinned by a mutable tag,
or drawing on a rolling snapshot, reconstructs at best a
functionally equivalent environment whose content may
have drifted. Even a correctly digest-pinned,
dated-snapshot rebuild is not guaranteed
byte-for-byte identical at the image level, because
per-layer timestamps ordinarily differ between builds.
Matching content is the guarantee a pinned recipe gives,
and bit-identical bytes require separate
reproducible-build tooling (@sec-containers). A team that treats the
pushed image as authoritative, and lets the Dockerfile
drift out of step with it, has converted its compendium
from something reconstructable into something that
merely happens to exist. The committed lockfile still
holds L1, but the environment layer is no longer
captured by anything the compendium contains, so the
compendium has regressed below L2. That regression is
what honest disclosure is meant to catch.

### Registries and the forge

Two distribution choices attend team sharing, and both
are concerns about vendor independence. Neither changes
the level a compendium has reached.

The **registry** is where the team image is published:
GitHub Container Registry, Docker Hub, or an
institutional registry such as one hosted inside GitLab.
Docker Hub is the most familiar. However, its free tier
rate-limits image pulls and permits only a single private
repository, constraints that a small laboratory reaches
quickly. GHCR integrates with the GitHub forge and has
more generous terms for public research. An institution
with confidentiality requirements may mandate a private
or self-hosted registry. The choice is a trade between
convenience and control, and, we would stress, it is
reversible. Because the guarantee is the Dockerfile, a
team can re-push its image to a different registry at any
time without altering the compendium.

The **forge** is where the repository and its continuous
integration live: GitHub, or, very often in the health
sciences, an institutional GitLab. This choice matters
because research compendia
are disproportionately authored on self-hosted GitLab.
Many universities and laboratories, particularly those
subject to on-premises data-governance rules, run their
own GitLab and cannot push to a public forge. A
framework whose premise is reproducibility for that
audience must not lock its users into one forge. The
practical difficulty is concentrated entirely in
continuous integration. GitHub Actions and GitLab CI use
structurally different configuration dialects. Supporting
both, without maintaining two parallel and divergent sets
of workflow files, therefore requires that the CI logic
be single-sourced, typically in the Makefile. Each
forge's configuration is then reduced to a thin shim that
calls it. The analyst should therefore treat the forge
as a replaceable host and keep the reproducibility logic
in artifacts that travel between forges unchanged.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: what survives a registry outage

A colleague argues that the team should push its image
to Docker Hub after every package installation, 'so the
image is always the source of truth'. What is wrong with
treating the pushed image as the source of truth, and
what should be the source of truth instead?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

The pushed image is an opaque, impermanent binary that
may be deleted, rate-limited, pruned, or built for the
wrong architecture. It cannot be inspected to see how it
was made. If Docker Hub removes it, an analysis that
depended on it is lost. The source of truth should be
the committed Dockerfile together with the lockfile it
restores from. That is a transparent, diffable, durable
recipe that reconstructs an identical image from pinned
inputs. The image is a convenience cache; the recipe is
the guarantee. Pushing after every install also wastes
effort, since the image need only be rebuilt
periodically from the union lockfile.
:::
:::

## Sharing with the world: archiving

Sharing with a team keeps a live project consistent.
Archiving asks a different question: how does a finished
compendium survive after the project ends, the
collaborators disperse, and the laboratory's servers are
decommissioned? A repository on a forge is not an
archive. Forges delete inactive accounts, rename
themselves, change ownership, and go out of business; a
URL that resolves today may not resolve in a decade. An
archive, by contrast, undertakes to preserve a deposit
and to keep a name for it resolving indefinitely.

The instrument is a deposit in a research repository
that mints a **persistent identifier**. Depositing the
compendium in Zenodo, the general-purpose repository
operated at CERN, produces a Digital Object Identifier.
The DOI continues to resolve even as the underlying
storage moves, and it can be cited in the article the
compendium supports. The DOI is what lifts a compendium
from merely locatable on a forge, which is fragile, to
durably findable, which is the archival requirement.

A deposit should carry the environment as well as the
source. Here the container runtimes of @sec-backends
supply the archival artifact needed. Apptainer, the
high-performance-computing runtime, builds a single
Singularity Image Format file from a digest-pinned Docker
image. That SIF, or equivalently an OCI image exported as
a tarball, is checksummable and depositable as one
object. The deposit needs one command,
`apptainer build env.sif docker://<image>@sha256:<digest>`,
which pulls the image by its digest, flattens its layers,
and writes them to a single read-only file. A reader who
skipped @sec-backends needs nothing more for this
chapter, and a reader without Apptainer can write the
tarball with Docker alone, using `docker save`. A
compendium archived as its source tree, a pinned
Dockerfile, and the built environment as a single file
is reproducible by two independent routes. A reader may
rebuild from the recipe or, if the
recipe's inputs have decayed, may run the archived
environment directly. Depositing both is belt and
suspenders, and for a result that matters it is worth
the disk. What a deposit may carry of the *data* is a
separate question. It is governed by the terms under
which the data were obtained, rather than by the
analyst's wish to be reproducible. For patient-level data
the usual answer is that the data stay out of an open
deposit, and @sec-restricted-deposit treats what is
deposited in their place.

These practices realize a set of principles that the
community has crystallized under the acronym FAIR.
Wilkinson and colleagues proposed that a research object
should be Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and
Reusable, and framed the principles for research data
[@wilkinson2016]. Barker and colleagues subsequently
adapted them for research software, whose reuse involves
execution as well as reading [@barker2022]. A DOI serves
findability. A repository with a stated access procedure
serves accessibility, which for restricted data means a
controlled route rather than an open download. A
documented, standard container format serves
interoperability, and a pinned, rebuildable environment
serves part of reusability. Reusability also requires a
clear usage license (R1.1 in the original principles),
which a pinned environment does not by itself supply. In
this light, the archetype-agnostic compendium of
@sec-compendium is most of the way to a FAIR object by
construction. This holds provided it is deposited rather
than merely committed and carries an explicit license;
licensing practice is treated separately.

### Licensing, CITATION.cff, and Software Heritage

A pinned environment and a minted DOI satisfy three of
FAIR's four letters without touching the fourth's hardest
requirement. Reusability, principle R1.1 in the original
statement, asks for 'a clear and accessible data usage
license' [@wilkinson2016]. Nothing about findability,
accessibility, or interoperability supplies one. A
compendium can be perfectly findable and still carry no
statement of what a reader is permitted to do with it.
In the absence of a license, that defaults, under
copyright, to nothing. 'The cohort, continued' below
returns to what license this book's own compendium
carries.

Two further instruments round out what a deposit should
carry, beyond the license file itself.

**CITATION.cff.** A `CITATION.cff` file is a plain-text,
machine-readable citation record placed at a repository's
root, using a small set of `key: value` fields
(`cff-version`, `authors`, `title`, `version`, and
`date-released` among them) [@githubcitationfiles2024].
GitHub parses the file, when it sits on the default branch,
into a 'Cite this repository' link on the repository page.
The link generates an APA or BibTeX citation on request
[@githubcitationfiles2024]. Zenodo can read the same file
when it archives a GitHub release and use it to pre-fill
the deposit's own citation metadata, so a `CITATION.cff`
written once serves both the forge and the archive. What
it pre-fills is only what the file says, the `license`
field included. A compendium with one license for its
prose and another for its code cannot record in that
field which license covers which files, so the license on
the resulting deposit is checked against `LICENSE` before
it is published. Without a `CITATION.cff`, a reader who wants to
cite the compendium constructs a citation by hand from
whatever metadata happens to be visible on the page. This
is the same fragility that motivated the DOI in the first
place.

**Software Heritage.** Zenodo is a deposit repository: an
institution, CERN, operates it. Its continuation is a
reasonable expectation, but it is an expectation and not
a guarantee, since a deposit repository could in
principle be discontinued by the institution that runs
it. Software Heritage undertakes something narrower and
more absolute for source code specifically. Its stated
mission is a permanent, universal archive of publicly
available source code, with no depositor-facing mechanism
to remove something once archived. The project's SWHID
identifier scheme was formalized as an ISO/IEC standard
in 2025 [@swhiso2025]. Every archived object, whether a
file, a directory, a commit, or a full repository
snapshot, receives a SoftWare Hash IDentifier of the form
`swh:1:<type>:<hash>`. Here `<type>` names the
kind of object (`cnt` for a file's content, `dir` for a
directory, among others) and `<hash>` is a 40-character
value computed from the object's own bytes
[@swhmodeldocs2024]. The identifier is computed from the
content rather than assigned by a registry. Two copies of
the same file anywhere in the archive therefore resolve
to the same SWHID. This is a different kind of guarantee
from a DOI: a DOI names a deposit, and a SWHID names the
bytes.



This book's own repository illustrates the gap between
having these instruments and using them well. A
`CITATION.cff` is
present at the
repository root, generated by zzcollab when the project
was created. Its `license` field reads
CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0, the license of the prose, while
`LICENSE` places all code under CC0; the file's abstract
states the dual licensing in words, but a deposit service
reading the `license` field sees only the one identifier.
Its `orcid` field is still empty, so the record names its author without a persistent identifier.
The file's presence is enough for GitHub to render the
'Cite this repository' link and for Zenodo to read it on
deposit. Whether its content credits the right people
under the right license is a question only a reading of
the file answers.

Two broader efforts merit the analyst's attention.
The Whole Tale platform, described by Brinckman and
colleagues, bundles code, data, and computational
environment into a single executable research object.
A reader can run it in the browser without local
installation [@brinckman2019], an ambition the
compendium-plus-archived-image pattern approaches by
other means. And the Turing Way, a community-authored
handbook, collects the collaborative and stewardship
practices of reproducible research into one continually
updated reference [@turingway2022]. Some readers will
want the social side of collaboration, from code review
to project governance to credit, in more depth than a
single chapter allows. They should begin there.

### When the data are restricted {#sec-restricted-deposit}

Everything said so far about depositing assumes that every
file in the compendium may be published. In health
research that assumption is usually false. A compendium
built on patient records contains, or was built from,
such data. Their release is governed by law, by the
consent the participants gave, and by the data-use
agreement under which the analyst received the extract.
A deposit in an
open repository is a publication to anyone, indefinitely,
and a file placed there cannot be recalled.

::: {.callout-important}
## Restricted data

The rule is the commit rule of @sec-version-control, made
stricter. Patient-level data do not go into an open
deposit unless three conditions hold. They must have been
formally de-identified, and the consent and the agreement
must both permit public release. The responsible data
steward or IRB must also have confirmed it in writing. In
their place, a deposit may take four routes:

- the code, the tests, the lockfile, the Dockerfile, and
  the archived image, always;
- de-identified data, only where the data's steward has
  made that determination;
- a synthetic stand-in, labeled as such;
- for data that may be shared under agreement but not
  opened to the world, a citation to a controlled-access
  repository such as dbGaP.

None of these substitutes removes the
obligation to read the consent form and the data-use
agreement first. The deposit's data-availability
statement must say, exactly, which of these routes was
taken.
:::

The paragraphs below work through each of the four routes
named above, and the two documents that govern the choice,
in enough detail to act on.

**The code and the environment, always.** The analysis
code, the tests, the lockfile, the Dockerfile, and the
archived image carry no participant data. Depositing
them openly lets anyone inspect the analysis, and lets
anyone who obtains the data by the legitimate route re-run
it. Two checks come first. The archived image must not
contain the data. A `COPY . .` executed while the extract
sat in the build context places it inside the image. A
`.dockerignore` that excludes the data directory, and an
inspection of the built image's file system, are
therefore part of the deposit. And the other artifacts
must not carry individual-level rows by another route.
Rendered reports, cached chunk output, saved workspaces,
logs, and test fixtures are all places where records
leak. Tables with very small cell counts can disclose as
surely as a row does.

**De-identified data, where permitted.** Under the HIPAA
Privacy Rule, health information ceases to be
individually identifiable by one of two routes. In the
first, a qualified expert applies statistical methods and
documents that the risk of identification is very small.
In the second, the eighteen listed identifiers are
removed and the covered entity has no actual knowledge
that the remainder could identify anyone [@cfr164514]. A
limited data set,
which keeps dates and some geography, is not
de-identified and may be shared only under a data-use
agreement [@cfr164514]. NIH guidance adds that data
de-identified in the legal sense may still warrant
controlled access [@nihprivacy2026]. De-identification is
a determination made by the data's steward, not something
an analyst achieves by deleting the name column.

**Synthetic data, as a stand-in.** A synthetic file with
the same columns, types, and plausible ranges as the
analysis data lets a reader run the pipeline from end to
end. The reader can confirm that the code executes,
though not that the published estimates regenerate. It
should be labeled
synthetic in the file and in the README, with the script
that generated it. A synthetic file produced by a model
fitted to the real records needs the same disclosure
review as the records themselves, since such a model can
reproduce rare individuals. One simulated from stated
parameters, as this book's running cohort is, does not.

**Controlled-access repositories.** When data may be
shared but not publicly, a controlled-access repository
holds them and releases them only to approved users under
an agreement. NIH's dbGaP, for genotype and phenotype
data, is an example: public study descriptions sit beside
an authorized-access route with its own security
procedures and code of conduct [@dbgap]. The open deposit
of code then cites the controlled-access accession, so
that the two halves are linked by identifier. The NIH Data
Management and Sharing Policy has been in force since 25
January 2023. It expects controlled access for data with
explicit limits on later use, and asks that those limits
be passed to the repository that holds the data
[@nihdms2020].

**Consent and agreement terms, read before the analysis
begins.** What may be deposited is settled by documents
signed long before the deposit: the consent form, the IRB
protocol, and the data-use agreement. The analyst reads
them for redistribution, derived data, public posting,
and retention. An agreement that requires the extract to
be destroyed at the end of the project governs every copy
of it, including those in backups, caches, and container
images. NIH guidance asks that consent explain how data
will be shared and that use agreements carry their
restrictions with the data [@nihdms2020; @nihprivacy2026].

**The data-availability statement.** The article and the
README state what was deposited, where, and how the rest
may be obtained, with the same exactness the honest-level
claim demands. A statement of the following form is
typical:

> The analysis code, package lockfile, container recipe,
> and archived container image are openly available at
> [DOI], with a synthetic dataset of the same structure
> on which the pipeline runs from end to end. The
> patient-level data were obtained from [registry] under
> a data-use agreement that does not permit
> redistribution; qualified researchers may apply to
> [data steward] for access. The synthetic data do not
> reproduce the reported estimates.

The last sentence bears on the level claim. A reader without
access to the data can confirm that the pipeline executes.
Only someone with access can confirm that it regenerates
the published numbers, so an L3 claim must say who
performed the comparison and on what data.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}

Deleting two columns is not de-identification in the
regulatory sense. Dates, small geography, and rare
combinations of remaining variables can still re-identify
a person. A determination that the risk is very small
must be made by a qualified expert or by removing all
eighteen HIPAA identifiers, not by the analyst's own
judgment. Absent that determination in writing from the
data steward or IRB, the extract stays out of an open
deposit. The appropriate route is a synthetic stand-in with
the same structure, deposited openly and labeled as
synthetic. The real extract is made available, if the
agreement allows it at all, only through a
controlled-access repository or a direct request to the
data steward.
:::
:::

### Funder and journal obligations

Everything the four routes above implement is a response
to an obligation that exists before the analysis begins:
a funder's data-sharing policy and, later, a journal's
reporting requirement. Both predate the deposit and
shape what the
deposit must contain.

**The funder side.** The NIH Data Management and Sharing
Policy applies to proposals due on or after 25
January 2023. It requires that an applicant submit a Data
Management and Sharing Plan at the time of application,
not drafted after data collection is underway
[@nihdms2020]. The Plan goes in the 'Other Plan(s)'
attachment of the research plan; only a brief summary
and the associated costs go in the budget and its
justification [@nihdmswriting]. NIH
program staff review the Plan for completeness rather
than scoring it. However, once an award is made, the
approved Plan becomes a term and condition of that award.
Noncompliance can bring added special terms, withheld
funds, or termination, and can affect future funding
decisions [@nihdms2020]. For the analyst, the choice
among the four routes above was therefore made, in
outline, when the grant was written; the deposit executes
the Plan.

**The journal side.** A code-availability statement is a
narrower instrument than the data-availability statement
of this section, above. It says where the *analysis code*
lives, under what license, at what version, and what it
does not include. It does so independently of whatever
the data-availability statement says about the data. The
two statements answer different questions, and a
manuscript needs both. A reader who wants to re-run the
pipeline reads the code statement, and a reader who wants
to obtain the inputs reads the data statement.

Some reporting guidelines now name code availability as a
checklist item rather than leaving it to a journal's
general policy. TRIPOD+AI is the 2024 extension of the
TRIPOD reporting guideline to prediction models built
with regression or machine learning. Under its 'Open
science' section it lists item 18f, 'Provide details of
the availability of the analytical code,' and adds a
footnote. The footnote specifies that this covers the
analysis code, including
any data cleaning, feature engineering, model building, and
evaluation [@collinstripodai2024]. A separate item, 18e,
asks the same question of the data. Naming code
availability as its own item, distinct from data
availability, is what makes TRIPOD+AI concrete where a
general journal policy is often vague: an author
completing the checklist cannot satisfy 18f by describing
only the data.

A code-availability statement that meets this bar states
four things. The first is where the code is deposited,
with a persistent identifier if one was minted. The
second is under what license it is released. The third
is which version, commit, or tagged release corresponds
to the reported results, since a repository's default
branch moves on after publication. The fourth is what,
if anything, the deposit withholds, and why (a
proprietary dependency, institution-licensed software, or
data referenced only by an accession number). 'Available
on GitHub,' without a version and a license, answers none
of the four.

## Stewardship over time

Archiving preserves the artifacts; stewardship is the
longer discipline of keeping them runnable as the world
underneath them changes. Even a carefully pinned
compendium decays. A base image tag may be re-pushed. A
package version pinned in a lockfile may age out of the
repository that once served it, and a system library may
be dropped from a new operating-system release. The
question stewardship answers is this. When the pins have
decayed and the archived image was lost or never built,
can the environment still be recovered?

For the R ecosystem a useful recovery tool is `rang`,
described by Chan and colleagues [@chan2023]. (`rang`
was archived on CRAN on 2026-08-22. The historical
versions remain installable from the CRAN archive or
from its GitHub repository. The technique it illustrates
is worth knowing even if the package itself needs an
alternative source or a successor tool by the time a
reader needs it.) The ordinary workflow pins
prospectively, by recording a lockfile at development
time and restoring from it. `rang`, by contrast,
reconstructs an environment retrospectively, from a
*date*. Given the date an analysis was run, it resolves
the package versions current on the archives at that
date. It then generates a Dockerfile that can often
reconstruct a period-correct environment even when no
original lockfile survives. The two approaches are
complementary on a time axis. The framework of this book
enforces consistency prospectively over a project's
active life, and `rang` provides a recovery path
retrospectively when that consistency has lapsed. A
prudent steward records the run date in the compendium so
that this recovery path stays open.

::: {.callout-important}
## The honest level

Sharing and archiving themselves reach no rung, since
preserving a level is not capturing or verifying one. The
single failure this chapter exists to prevent is depositing
a compendium no better than locatable, with a DOI and a
tidy README, and calling it 'fully reproducible' in the
article the deposit outlives.
:::

We must extend the same honesty to the tools this book
has taught, and to the framework it uses as its running
example. Frameworks that compose the whole determinant
stack are young. Measured against the
9 layers of the determinant
stack in @sec-levels, the framework firmly pins roughly
four: the operating system and system libraries, the R
runtime, the package versions, and the analysis code,
with much of the session configuration besides. It
leaves the rest (the hardware, the numerical libraries,
the input data, and intrinsic non-determinism) to the
base image, to the analyst, or to convention. Its own
system review describes it candidly as a strong
scaffolding tool rather than a finished guarantor of reproducibility. The review also notes the
sustainability risk that attends a small maintainer
base: a single principal author is a bus factor of one,
and the tool's future depends on that one person.
The appropriate response is to disclose its reach
accurately, the same discipline the honest-level callout
demands of any analysis. The evidence that disclosure
cannot be taken for granted is empirical. Stodden and
colleagues examined the effectiveness of journal
reproducibility policies. They found that the mere
existence of a policy is a weak predictor of an actually
reproducible artifact [@stodden2018]. A gap between the
reproducibility a project claims and the reproducibility
it delivers is common.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}

:::
:::

## Across the archetypes

We turn now to how the machinery varies, or does not,
across the archetypes. The team and archiving machinery
is archetype-agnostic: the two-layer model, the union
lockfile, the registry and forge choices, the DOI
deposit, and the `rang` recovery path apply to every
archetype; @tbl-archetype-weight in @sec-compendium is
the reference. What varies is the final act of
publication. A **data-analysis** or **simulation**
compendium is deposited as itself: the compendium with
its DOI *is* the published object. A **manuscript**
compendium is deposited *beside* the article it supports,
cited by DOI from its data-availability statement. A
**package** compendium has a further, ecosystem-native
channel, release to CRAN or an R-universe, whose incoming
checks are themselves a validation gate. A **blog**
compendium is deployed as a website, with tools such as
`workflowr` [@blischak2019] binding each rendered page to
the commit that produced it. The archival obligation
still applies to the compendium behind the posts. In
every case the underlying discipline is identical: fix
the environment, govern it as a team, deposit with a
persistent identifier, and state the level honestly.
Only the last mile differs.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}

## Answer

statement of the level reached. It does not
need @sec-restricted-deposit's machinery at all. Data
generated by the study's own code from stated parameters
carries no participant, no consent, and no data-use
agreement to honor.
:::
:::

## Worked example

To make the abstractions concrete, we follow the
multi-site cohort laboratory of the Orientation through
one quarter of collaboration and one archival deposit.

At the project's start the lead selected a base image,
resolved it to a digest, and built the team environment
once. Over the quarter, three contributors extended the
package layer independently. The union model records the
result: the project lockfile always holds the union of
every contributor's additions. The following chunk
reconstructs the running union over the quarter and
tabulates it. It uses only base R together with `tibble`
and `knitr`, and computes the cumulative union
deterministically, so it regenerates identically on
every render.


::: {#tbl-union .cell tbl-cap='The renv union model over one quarter of team collaboration. Each contributor installs packages independently; the project lockfile records the cumulative union, which the shared image is periodically rebuilt from. Because it is a union rather than a running total, a package a contributor installs that another already has does not enlarge it, so the union can grow by fewer than the number of packages added. The union size never shrinks, so every contributor who rebuilds inherits the full set.'}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(tibble)
library(knitr)

contributions <- tibble::tribble(
  ~contributor,          ~added,
  'Lead (initial base)', 'here, renv, rmarkdown',
  'Ana (survival)',      'survival, survminer, here',
  'Ben (tables)',        'gtsummary, gt',
  'Cai (spatial)',       'sf, tmap'
)

added_sets <- strsplit(contributions$added, ', ')
running_union <- Reduce(union, added_sets,
                        accumulate = TRUE)

contributions$union_n <- vapply(
  running_union, length, integer(1)
)

knitr::kable(
  contributions[, c('contributor', 'added', 'union_n')],
  col.names = c('Contributor', 'Packages added',
                'Lockfile union (n)')
)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


|Contributor         |Packages added            | Lockfile union (n)|
|:-------------------|:-------------------------|------------------:|
|Lead (initial base) |here, renv, rmarkdown     |                  3|
|Ana (survival)      |survival, survminer, here |                  5|
|Ben (tables)        |gtsummary, gt             |                  7|
|Cai (spatial)       |sf, tmap                  |                  9|


:::
:::


We see in the table the invariant that makes the model
work. The union size is monotone, never shrinking as
contributors are added, so a member who rebuilds the
image at any point inherits everything the team needs up
to that point. Because it is a union and not a running
total, a package a contributor installs that the team
already has does not enlarge it. Ana adds
3 packages, but one of them,
`here`, was already in the lockfile from the initial
base. The union therefore grows by only
2,
from 3 to
5. Ana never installs `sf`,
yet after
the quarterly rebuild her environment carries it, because
Cai did, and the lockfile records the union.

When the manuscript was accepted, the laboratory
deposited the compendium. The cohort's patient-level
extract came from the participating sites under a
data-use agreement that forbids redistribution. The
deposit therefore follows @sec-restricted-deposit. It
carries the code, the tests, the lockfile, the
Dockerfile, the archived environment, and a synthetic
extract with the structure of the real one. It also
carries a README whose data-availability statement names
the sites' data steward as the route to the real data.
The extract itself is in none of these files. The session
below is shown as a static illustration rather than
executed. It checks that the image holds no study data,
publishes it to a registry, and records its immutable
digest. It then exports the environment as a single
archival file and mints a DOI for the compendium. The `$`
prompt is not part of the commands, and lines beginning
`#>` are output.

```bash
# Rebuild the team image once, from the pinned
# Dockerfile and the union lockfile, then publish it.
$ make docker-build

# Before the image leaves the laboratory, confirm that
# no study data were copied into it; the expected
# result is an empty listing.
$ docker run --rm cohort-env:latest \
    find / -xdev -path '*raw_data*' -type f

$ docker tag cohort-env:latest \
    ghcr.io/mylab/cohort-env:2026-q3
$ docker push ghcr.io/mylab/cohort-env:2026-q3

# Record the immutable digest the team builds against.
# This, not the mutable tag, is the reproducible name.
$ docker inspect --format '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' \
    ghcr.io/mylab/cohort-env:2026-q3
#> ghcr.io/mylab/cohort-env@sha256:4813816ad695...

# Export the environment as a single archival file for
# deposit, built from the digest-pinned image.
$ apptainer build cohort-env.sif \
    docker://ghcr.io/mylab/cohort-env@sha256:4813816ad695...

# Deposit the compendium (code, tests, lockfile,
# Dockerfile, synthetic extract, README; no patient
# data) plus the archived environment in Zenodo, which
# mints the persistent identifier the article's
# data-availability statement will cite. The command is
# schematic; real deposition uses the Zenodo REST API or
# the web upload interface, and the DOI is a placeholder.
$ zenodo-upload cohort-compendium-v1.0.zip cohort-env.sif  # schematic
#> Deposited. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.XXXXXXX
```

Three features of the session deserve note. First, the
image is pushed by a dated tag but *recorded* by digest;
the tag is convenient for humans, the digest is the
immutable name a collaborator or a reviewer builds
against. Second, the deposit carries both the compendium
and the archived environment. Reproduction therefore has
two independent routes, rebuild-from-recipe and
run-the-archived-image, and does not depend on the
registry surviving. Third, neither route includes the
patient data. A reader of the deposit can run the
pipeline on the synthetic extract and see that it
executes. Regenerating the published estimates requires
the real extract, obtained under the sites' agreement,
and the article's level claim says so.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: two routes, one reason

The deposit above includes both a rebuildable Dockerfile
and an archived SIF file of the same environment. Why
both, rather than whichever is more convenient?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

Because each route can fail independently, and the
deposit is meant to outlive both failures. The Dockerfile
route fails if the base image's registry disappears or a
pinned package is pulled from CRAN before `rang` or a
successor tool can recover it. The archived-image route
fails if the SIF or OCI file itself is lost or becomes
unreadable by a future runtime. Depositing both means a
reader needs only one of the two to still work. The
archived image is often a gigabyte or more, so the
second route is not free, but for a result that matters
it is worth its size.
:::
:::

## The cohort, continued

The worked example above is a composite laboratory. We
now apply a smaller, real question to this book's own
running cohort compendium. If it had to be deposited
today, what would already be true, and what would still
need doing?


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
repo <- '../..'
in_repo <- function(path) file.exists(file.path(repo, path))

license_present <- in_repo('LICENSE')
description_present <- in_repo('DESCRIPTION')
lockfile_present <- in_repo('renv.lock')
dockerfile_present <- in_repo('Dockerfile')
dockerignore_present <- in_repo('.dockerignore')

# Ask git itself, so that directory patterns and `!`
# exceptions are applied exactly as `git add` applies them.
git_ignores <- function(path) {
  if (!nzchar(Sys.which('git'))) return(NA)
  status <- system2(
    'git',
    c('-C', repo, 'check-ignore', '--no-index', '--quiet', path),
    stdout = FALSE, stderr = FALSE
  )
  if (status %in% c(0L, 1L)) status == 0L else NA
}
cohort_ignored <- git_ignores('analysis/data/raw_data/cohort_raw.csv')
second_file_ignored <- git_ignores(
  'analysis/data/raw_data/registry_extract_2027.csv'
)

cff_lines <- readLines(file.path(repo, 'CITATION.cff'))
cff_license <- sub('^license:\\s*', '',
                   grep('^license:', cff_lines, value = TRUE))

level_now <- if (lockfile_present && dockerfile_present) {
  'L2'
} else if (lockfile_present) {
  'L1'
} else {
  'L0'
}
c(LICENSE = license_present,
  DESCRIPTION = description_present,
  renv.lock = lockfile_present,
  Dockerfile = dockerfile_present,
  .dockerignore = dockerignore_present,
  cohort_csv_ignored = cohort_ignored,
  second_file_ignored = second_file_ignored)
#>             LICENSE         DESCRIPTION           renv.lock          Dockerfile 
#>                TRUE                TRUE                TRUE               FALSE 
#>       .dockerignore  cohort_csv_ignored second_file_ignored 
#>               FALSE                TRUE                TRUE
```
:::




The first two checks concern licensing. A `LICENSE` file
is present, and
it is dual: the prose is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 and the code,
including every script that builds the cohort, is CC0.
That is the explicit license FAIR's reusability principle
asks for, and the one @sec-restricted-deposit's deposit
example above was silent about. A `DESCRIPTION` file is
present and
records `License: CC0`, matching the code half of the
`LICENSE` file, so a package repository or an automated
check reading `DESCRIPTION` sees the same answer for the
code that a human reading `LICENSE` would. `CITATION.cff`
does not: its single `license` field reads
CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0, the prose license, and a deposit
service that takes its license from that field would
record it for the code as well. Before a deposit, the
license recorded in the deposit's own metadata is checked
by hand against `LICENSE`.

The last two checks ask git itself, through
`git check-ignore`, whether a path would be ignored. The
cohort extract `analysis/data/raw_data/cohort_raw.csv` is
ignored.
The more informative result is the second. The file
`registry_extract_2027.csv` does not exist and is named
nowhere in `.gitignore`, yet git reports that a file of
that name placed in the same directory would be
ignored as well.
This is what protects real data. A rule that names one
file protects that file and nothing else, and the next
extract a teammate saves beside it under a new name would
be staged by the next `git add .` without a warning. The
directory pattern `analysis/data/raw_data/*`, with an
exception for the directory's `README.md`, protects
whatever is put in the directory, including files no one
has yet thought to name. A text search of `.gitignore`
for the string `raw_data` cannot tell these two cases
apart, which is why the chunk asks git rather than
reading the file, and why it tests a filename that
appears nowhere in it. The CSV itself is generated from a
committed script rather than tracked. This is the
practice that the version-control chapter
(@sec-version-control) and @sec-restricted-deposit both
prescribe for data with identifier-shaped columns. The
chunk cannot certify whether the data are actually
sensitive, only which paths git would exclude. That
judgment is the analyst's, informed by what the data are.

On the capture ladder, the compendium is at L1.
What it still lacks among the artifacts checked here is a `Dockerfile` and a `.dockerignore`.
The `.dockerignore` matters as soon as a `Dockerfile`
exists, because `.gitignore` keeps files out of git and
not out of a Docker build context; Exercise 8 below
follows a file through that gap. What the compendium
still lacks for an archival deposit proper is the part no
file-system check can see. It lacks a minted DOI, an
archived container image, and a written statement of the
level this compendium has reached at the time of deposit.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}

Suppose every check above returned `TRUE` for this
compendium, a `Dockerfile` and a `.dockerignore`
included. Would that mean the compendium is ready to
deposit as L3? Why or why not?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

No. The checks are structural: a license file exists, a
`DESCRIPTION` agrees with it, the capture files exist,
and git would exclude the data directory. None of
them is evidence that the analysis has been rebuilt from a
clean environment and its outputs compared against a
committed baseline within a stated tolerance. That is
what an L3 claim requires. A
compendium can pass every structural check above and
still be no higher than L2, because files that capture
the environment are not evidence that anyone rebuilt it.
Structural readiness for deposit and
the level honestly claimed in the deposit are two different
questions, and this section answers only the first.
:::
:::

## Collaborating with an LLM

A language model is a capable assistant for the
mechanical parts of sharing and archiving. It is an
unreliable one for the parts that require judgment about
this specific project.

## Restricted data

One rule comes first (habit 3). Never paste or upload
protected health information, identifiable records, or data
held under a data use agreement, nor outputs derived from
them, into a model or a coding agent unless three conditions
all hold. The institution has approved that endpoint for
that class of data. The IRB protocol and the consent permit
the processing. The data use agreement, or the provider's
terms, permits it. If any of the three is unclear, the
answer is no.

The third condition is the one most often missed.
Institutional approval of a tool does not override the terms
under which a data provider released the data. NIH, for
example, treats sharing controlled-access data with
third-party generative AI tools through prompts as a breach
of the data use certification, and a model trained on such
data as a derivative that may not be distributed without
approval [@nihgenai2025].

Describe the structure instead: the column names and types,
or a small synthetic example generated from the data
dictionary, never edited from real rows. A coding agent sees
whatever files are in its working tree, so run it in a
checkout or container where the real data is not mounted.
:::


For a deposit, the derived outputs that fall under the rule
include row-level logs and small-count tables, and the
NIH policy cited above applies to any third-party
generative AI tool, not only to public ones. A prompt about
a deposit names the file names and the directory layout
rather than any file's contents. We give three exchanges,
each with what to watch for and what the analyst must
verify.

**Prompt.** 'Write the shell commands to tag our image,
push it to GHCR, record its digest, and export it as a
SIF for archival deposit.'

*Watch for.* A model will readily produce plausible
commands. However, it may push and record the *mutable
tag* rather than resolving and recording the *digest*.
That silently discards the reproducibility the exercise
exists to secure. It may also invent registry paths or
flags that do not exist for the analyst's setup.

*Verification.* Run each command and confirm the recorded
reference is a `@sha256:...` digest, not a `:tag`. Pull
the image fresh on a second machine using the recorded
digest and confirm it resolves. Do not deposit until the
digest round-trips.

**Prompt.** 'Draft the data-availability and
reproducibility statement for our manuscript, citing the
deposited compendium.'

*Watch for.* The model does not know what level the
compendium actually reached, and will tend to reach for
confident language ('fully reproducible', 'all results
can be regenerated') regardless. It cannot know whether
the analyst verified the outputs or merely pinned them.
Nor does it know the terms of the data-use agreement, and it will
often write 'all data are available in the deposited
compendium' for a deposit that holds none.

*Verification.* Rewrite the level claim by hand against
the honest-level standard. Say verified only if
`zzc verify` or its equivalent was run and its baseline
test passed; say pinned if the environment was pinned
but not re-run. Name the DOI actually minted, not a
placeholder. Check every
sentence about the data against what the deposit holds
and against the agreement, and name the access route for
anything withheld.

**Prompt.** 'Our 2024 analysis has an renv.lock but
several pinned versions no longer install. How do we
reproduce it?'

*Watch for.* The model may confidently propose editing
the lockfile to newer versions, which changes the
analysis rather than reproducing it. It may also
recommend `rang` but misstate what input it needs.

*Verification.* Confirm that the proposed route
reconstructs the *original* versions from the recorded
run date. Test the reconstructed environment against a
known output from the original analysis before trusting
it.

## Exercise 1

No single correct answer. The criterion to apply is
**how often the package changes and how many contributors
need it**.

The **environment layer** is the team image. Beyond the
operating system, R, and the system libraries, it holds
the packages every project needs and nobody changes: the
tidyverse, `knitr` and `rmarkdown`, the
plotting stack, anything requiring system libraries that
are expensive to install. Baking these into the image means
each contributor pays the install cost zero times rather
than once each. The layer moves only when the team lead
rebuilds.

The **package layer** holds what one contributor needs for
one piece of work: a specialized survival package, a
mapping library used in a single figure, anything adopted
mid-project. These arrive through the lockfile, which every
contributor extends.

**The borderline cases** are the substance of the exercise,
and three kinds recur.

A package that *started* in the package layer and is now
used by everyone belongs in the environment layer at the
next rebuild. The signal is the union model: when a package
appears in the lockfile because several contributors
installed it independently, it has outgrown the fast layer.

A package with heavy system dependencies used by only one
contributor is ambiguous. Installing it from the
lockfile is slow and may fail without the system libraries;
baking it in imposes the size on everyone. The usual
resolution is to put the *system libraries* in the image
and leave the R package in the lockfile.

A package pinned to an unusual version for one analysis
belongs in that project's package layer, however widely
the package itself is used. The team image serves every
project in the lab and should carry the version most of
them use. One project's lockfile can record the unusual
version and restore it into the project library, which
takes precedence over the image's copy, without imposing
it on the other projects. Within a single project the
union lockfile still records one version per package, so
that project's contributors must agree on it.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 2

A paragraph a collaborator could act on:

> The Dockerfile is a recipe and the image is a
> cake. The recipe says how the environment was made,
> in text, in version control, reviewable line by line,
> and it will still say so in ten years. The image is an
> opaque binary that someone must keep hosting. It can be
> deleted, pruned, rate-limited, or rebuilt under the same
> tag, and nothing in it explains how it was produced. So
> commit the Dockerfile and treat the pushed image as a
> cache: convenient, worth having, and not the record.

**A concrete failure from relying on the pushed image.**
Docker Hub applies a retention policy to inactive
repositories and the image is removed. Alternatively, the
organization account lapses, or the tag is overwritten by
a later push.
An analysis whose only environment record was that image
is now unreconstructable. The failure appears at exactly
the moment someone tries to reproduce the work, which is
usually years after anyone was watching.

A second and more insidious failure merits mention
because it produces no error. The image is rebuilt and
pushed under the same tag with a newer base. A reader pulls
the tag, gets a different environment from the one the
analysis ran in, and obtains slightly different numbers
with nothing to indicate anything moved. This is the
argument for pinning by digest as well as committing the
recipe.

A third arises if the collaborator works on Apple
Silicon. The pushed image may have been built for one
architecture only. The pull then succeeds on the author's
machine and fails, or runs under emulation with different
numerical behavior, on someone else's.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 3

**What must change.** The CI configuration file, from
`.github/workflows/*.yml` to a single `.gitlab-ci.yml` at
the root, in the dialect of stages and scripts rather than
jobs and reusable actions. The remote URL and the
authentication method. The registry, from GHCR to the
GitLab container registry, and therefore the image
reference in any pull. The secrets, which must be
re-created as GitLab CI variables. Anything relying on a
GitHub-specific feature: pull-request comment bots,
`GITHUB_TOKEN`, Actions from the marketplace.

**What does not change.** Everything that constitutes the
reproducibility of the compendium. The Dockerfile, the
`renv.lock`, the directory structure, the `DESCRIPTION`,
the tests, the analysis code, the data dictionary, and the
checks themselves are all forge-agnostic. (Restricted
data stay off both forges; moving forges does not change
where they live.) The reproducibility machinery is
independent of the hosting platform. A compendium that
must be substantially rewritten to move forges was coupled
to its forge in ways it should not have been.

**Where the CI logic should live.** In a `Makefile`, or an
equivalent single entry point, so that both forges' CI
files reduce to a shim naming an image and calling
`make check`, `make check-renv`, and the render target
that matches the archetype (`make docker-render` for an
`.Rmd` report; there is no plain `make render`). The
migration then touches one thin file rather than the
check logic, and the same commands run locally. That
incidental benefit makes the arrangement worth adopting
even for a project that will never move.
:::

For the registry case, the deposit loses the data and the
statement gains an access route:

> The analysis code, package lockfile, container recipe,
> and archived container image are archived at
> https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.XXXXXXX, with a synthetic
> dataset of the same structure on which the pipeline
> runs from end to end. The patient-level data were
> obtained from [registry] under a data-use agreement
> that does not permit redistribution; qualified
> researchers may apply to [data steward] for access. The
> synthetic data do not reproduce the reported estimates.
> The environment is pinned (L2); re-execution on the
> registry data has not been independently verified.

A common wrong answer keeps 'the complete research
compendium' in the second statement. It is not complete,
and saying so is part of the statement's honesty.

**Defending the claim against the honest-level standard**
means checking three things and being willing to have the
answer come out lower than one would like. Is there a
lockfile? Then L1. Is there, in addition, an artifact
pinning the runtime and system libraries? Then L2. Is
there *evidence* (a CI log or a verification report) that
a baseline test passed within a stated tolerance after a
clean rebuild? Only then L3. A recorded hash of an output
file is not that evidence. A matching hash shows that the
file has not changed, but L3 is defined by agreement with
a committed baseline within a tolerance, which a hash
cannot express.

The last clause of the statement above is the one that
makes it honest, and it is the clause most authors omit.
Omitting it invites the reader to assume verification
that nobody performed.
:::

## Exercise 5

```r
lockfile <- renv::lockfile_read('renv.lock')
pkg_names <- names(lockfile$Packages)

graph <- rang::resolve(pkg_names, snapshot_date = '2026-06-29')
rang::dockerize(graph, output_dir = 'rang_build')
```

The comparison typically shows most packages matching and
a minority differing, with the differing set growing as
the gap widens between the snapshot date and the dates on
which packages were actually installed.

**Why a date-based reconstruction may not match a
lockfile exactly.** Four reasons, and it is worth
separating them.

First and most important, a lockfile records what was
*installed*, and a date reconstruction records what was
*current on a date*. These differ whenever a package was
installed on one date and the lockfile written on another.
That is the normal case for a project of any duration.

Second, packages installed from sources other than CRAN
(from GitHub at a particular commit, or from Bioconductor)
have no CRAN-dated equivalent. The reconstruction
therefore either misses them or substitutes something.

Third, archived packages present a gap. A package removed
from CRAN is recoverable from the archive by version, but
its dependency resolution at a past date may not be.

Fourth, the reconstruction resolves the transitive closure
afresh, so a dependency that has since changed its own
requirements can pull a different set than the lockfile
recorded.

The conclusion the chapter draws: reconstruction by date
is what one falls back on when no lockfile exists, and it
is an approximation rather than a substitute. A project
with a lockfile should restore it.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}

Taking each in turn; the reader needs only one.

**R package.** The sharing step beyond the deposit is

Bioconductor, or at minimum a tagged release installable
with `remotes::install_github()`. The validation gate this
adds is substantial and externally imposed. CRAN runs

including development R, and rejects the package on
failure. This is a stronger gate than any the author
configured, precisely because the author did not configure
it. It is the closest thing in the R ecosystem to the
independent verification of @sec-verification.

**Blog.** The step is deployment to a public URL with a
feed, and registration where readers will find it. The
gate added is thin: a deploy check confirming the site
builds and links resolve. Notably, no gate checks that the
code in the posts still runs. That is why an old post is
the most reliably broken artifact in this book's
taxonomy.

**Simulation study.** The step is depositing the full
results alongside the reduced pipeline, together with the
seed and the replicate count, since the full run is too
expensive to reproduce on demand. The gate added is the
correspondence check: the reduced pipeline under the
recorded seed must regenerate the leading replicates of
the deposited full results. That is what lets a reader
verify the machinery without paying for the study.

**At `docker build`.** The build context includes every
file under the Dockerfile's directory not excluded by
`.dockerignore`. Because `*.csv` does not match
`extra.tsv`, the file is copied into the image by any
`COPY . .` or equivalent instruction. It thereby becomes
part of the image's file system layers.

**At `docker push`.** The image, `.tsv` included, is
uploaded to the registry as-is. The registry has no
knowledge of which files are data and which are code; it
stores the layers it is given. The leak has now left the
laboratory's own machines.

**At the Zenodo deposit.** `apptainer build` exports the
pushed image, `.tsv` and all, into the SIF file, which is
then deposited and assigned a DOI. The leak is now public
and, per this chapter's own account of archival deposits,
unrecallable.

**What would have caught it.** An inspection of the built
image's file system before the push. This is the check
this chapter's worked example performs with `docker run
--rm ... find / -xdev -path '*raw_data*' -type f`, run
against the actual data directory rather than assumed from
the `.dockerignore` pattern. A pattern-matching ignore file
is a plan; a listing of what the built image actually
contains is a verification. Only the second one catches
a file the plan did not anticipate. This is the Verification
callout's own rule, 'how to see a claim actually holds,'
applied to the narrower claim that no data entered the
image.

## Cheat sheet {#sec-cheat-archiving}

| Command or rule | What it does or checks |
|---|---|
| `docker inspect --format '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' <img>` | Reports the immutable digest to record, not the mutable tag |
| `docker run --rm <img> find / -xdev -path '*raw_data*'` | Confirms no restricted data were copied into the built image |
| `apptainer build out.sif docker://<img>@sha256:...` | Exports a digest-pinned image as a single archival file |
| `renv.lock` + `Dockerfile`, committed | The reproducibility guarantee; the pushed image is a cache, not the record |
| Two-layer model | The team image (operating system, R, system libraries, lab-wide packages) is lead-governed and slow; the project lockfile is contributor-governed and fast, under the union model |
| Union lockfile | Records every contributor's packages cumulatively; never shrinks unless deliberately pruned; rebuild periodically, not on every install |
| `rang::resolve(pkgs, snapshot_date = ...)` | Reconstructs a period-correct environment from a date when no lockfile survives |
| Recorded run date | The single fact a retrospective recovery (`rang`) needs most |
| Restricted data (@sec-restricted-deposit) | Code and environment, always; data only de-identified, synthetic, or controlled-access, per the agreement (habit 3) |
| DOI deposit | Lifts a compendium from fragile-locatable (a forge URL) to durably findable; changes no rung on the ladder |
| Honest claim at deposit | State the rung actually reached; the deposit outlives the memory of what was done (habit 7) |

## Further reading

- Wilkinson and colleagues [@wilkinson2016] formulate
  the FAIR principles for research data; Barker and
  colleagues [@barker2022] adapt them for research
  software, whose reuse involves execution. Read both to
  understand what an archival deposit is trying to
  achieve, and why software reuse asks more than data
  reuse.
- Brinckman and colleagues [@brinckman2019] describe the
  Whole Tale platform, which bundles code, data, and
  environment into a single executable research object.
  It is the most ambitious realization of the
  compendium-as-runnable-object idea.
- The Turing Way [@turingway2022] is the community
  handbook for reproducible and collaborative research.
  For the social side of team collaboration, project
  governance, credit, and code review, in more depth
  than this chapter offers, it is the place to begin.
- Chan and colleagues [@chan2023] present `rang`, the
  retrospective recovery tool for decayed R
  environments. Read it together with the pinning of
  @sec-dependencies to see prospective capture and
  retrospective recovery as two halves of stewardship.
- Blischak and colleagues [@blischak2019] describe
  `workflowr`, which binds each rendered page of a
  versioned analysis website to its commit, the natural
  tool for the blog archetype's deployment.
- Stodden and colleagues [@stodden2018] provide the
  empirical case that a reproducibility policy is a weak
  predictor of an actually reproducible artifact, the
  evidence behind this book's insistence on honest
  disclosure over asserted reproducibility.
- The NIH Data Management and Sharing Policy
  [@nihdms2020] and NIH's principles for protecting
  participant privacy [@nihprivacy2026] set out what a
  funded project must plan for when its data come from
  human participants; read them before writing a
  data-availability statement for such a project.

## In conclusion

The book's argument comes down to four points.
Reproducibility, we have maintained throughout,
is not a badge a project either holds or lacks. It is a
level a project reaches. The discipline is to reach as
high as the work warrants and to say plainly how high
that was.

First, reproducibility comes in degrees, and the ladder
names them: locatable (L0), pinned packages (L1), pinned
environment (L2), and verified (L3). Every chapter of
this book has been an ascent of that ladder. We began by
finding the source and pinning the packages with a
lockfile. We then fixed the environment with a container
or a content-addressed alternative, and finally
regenerated the outputs and confirmed they match. The
ladder is the common scale on which any analysis, built
with any toolchain, can be placed and compared.

Second, the rungs are reached by two different kinds of
work, and conflating them is the source of much
confusion. Capture fixes the inputs and sets the level
from L0 to L2. Pinning the packages and the environment
is capture, which carries a compendium as far as L2. The
last rung, L3, is reached not by capture but by an act
of verification: a clean rebuild after which a baseline
test passes within a stated tolerance. Running
`zzc verify` once, with such a baseline test in place,
is therefore what lifts a pinned L2 compendium to a
verified L3 one. Automated re-checking is
distinct from that act. Continuous integration reruns the
verification on every change and certifies that the L3
state still holds, but it adds no rung of its own.
Removing it does not lower the level; it only stops the
automated confirmation. Keeping these registers distinct
is what lets a project report, honestly and
mechanically, exactly where it stands.

Third, the unit of reproducible work is the research
compendium, and it is not only a manuscript. The same
machinery, the same pillars, and the same ladder serve a
data analysis, a simulation study, an R package, a blog,
and a scholarly manuscript alike. The archetypes differ
only in their directory layout, in whether a report is
rendered, and in the last mile of publication: a package
submission, a deployed website, or a deposit beside an
article.

Fourth, and above all, the goal is reproducibility
matched honestly to the level actually reached. The
tools this book has taught, and the framework it has used
as its running example, are strong but partial. They
firmly secure some determinants and leave others to
convention, and an honest practitioner discloses the
difference. A verified L3 compendium and a locatable L0
script are both legitimate outputs of a scientific
process; what is not legitimate is to present the second
as the first. The reader who finishes this book with the
judgment to name the level a given analysis has reached,
across whatever archetype the work takes, and the
honesty to claim no more, has learned the one thing the
book most wished to teach.

## Seven habits, and a motto

*Claim only the level you have verified.*

1. Commit before you compute.
2. Pin what you ran, not what is current.
3. Never commit, deposit, or paste restricted data.
4. Make every gate able to fail, and watch it fail once.
5. Compare against a recorded baseline, with a stated tolerance.
6. Rebuild from clean, on a machine that is not yours.
7. Write the honest level down.
